hook.text: A website gets hacked every 39 seconds on average. It happens far more than people realize.

buildup.text: Attackers want data, money, computing power, or simply the thrill of breaking in.

discovery.text: Most attacks aren't personal. Automated bots scan the entire web for known vulnerabilities.

twist.text: Small sites aren't safer. Bots don't check your traffic — they check your software version.

climax.text: Every website is a target. Security isn't optional, no matter how small or obscure the site.

punchline.text: Bots don't care how small your site is.

quiz.question: How often does a website get hacked on average?

hook.text: The same ten types of vulnerabilities account for most web security breaches worldwide.

buildup.text: OWASP publishes a list of the most critical web application security risks every few years.

discovery.text: Injection, broken auth, and misconfiguration have topped the list for over a decade.

twist.text: The list barely changes between editions. The industry keeps making the same mistakes.

climax.text: OWASP Top Ten is the minimum every web developer should understand about security.

punchline.text: The same ten flaws haunt the web for decades.

quiz.question: What does OWASP publish?
options: A list of top web security risks

hook.text: Every form, API endpoint, and file upload is a door an attacker might try to open.

buildup.text: The attack surface is the total set of points where an unauthorized user can try to enter.

discovery.text: More features mean more surface area. Every new endpoint is another potential vulnerability.

twist.text: Forgotten admin panels and old API versions are some of the most exploited entry points.

climax.text: Reducing your attack surface — removing what you don't need — is the first line of defense.

punchline.text: Less surface area means fewer ways in.

quiz.question: What is an attack surface?
options: All points where attackers can try to enter

hook.text: The easiest way to break into a system is to trick a human into opening the door.

buildup.text: Phishing emails mimic trusted brands and lure users into entering passwords on fake sites.

discovery.text: Even experienced developers fall for well-crafted phishing attacks that mimic real workflows.

twist.text: Over 90% of data breaches start with a phishing email, not a technical exploit.

climax.text: The weakest link in web security is always the human being sitting at the keyboard.

punchline.text: Hackers hack people, not just computers.

quiz.question: What percentage of breaches start with phishing?

hook.text: Modern websites depend on hundreds of third-party packages. Each one is a trust decision.

buildup.text: A supply chain attack compromises a dependency that thousands of projects rely on.

discovery.text: The event-stream npm package was hijacked in 2018 to steal Bitcoin from a specific wallet.

twist.text: The attacker gained trust by maintaining the package for months before inserting malicious code.

climax.text: Every npm install is an act of trust. Supply chain security is now a critical web concern.

punchline.text: Your dependencies are someone else's code.

quiz.question: What is a supply chain attack?
options: Compromising a dependency others rely on

hook.text: What if an attacker could run their JavaScript inside your website, as if you wrote it?

buildup.text: XSS happens when a site displays user input without sanitizing it first.

discovery.text: An attacker injects a script tag into a comment field. Every visitor's browser executes it.

twist.text: XSS can steal cookies, redirect users, or impersonate them — all silently.

climax.text: XSS has been in the OWASP Top Ten since its first edition. It remains devastatingly common.

punchline.text: Never trust user input — ever.

quiz.question: What causes XSS vulnerabilities?

hook.text: A login form asks for a username. An attacker types SQL code instead of a name.

buildup.text: If the server builds queries by concatenating user input, that SQL code executes directly.

discovery.text: One crafted input can dump entire databases, delete tables, or bypass authentication.

twist.text: SQL injection was discovered in 1998. Over 25 years later, it still causes major breaches.

climax.text: Parameterized queries prevent SQL injection completely. The fix is simple — but often forgotten.

punchline.text: A 25-year-old bug still breaks websites daily.

quiz.question: What prevents SQL injection?

hook.text: You're logged into your bank. You visit a malicious site. It submits a transfer on your behalf.

buildup.text: CSRF tricks your browser into making authenticated requests to sites you're already logged into.

discovery.text: The attack works because browsers automatically send cookies with every request to a domain.

twist.text: CSRF tokens — unique values per form — stop the attack by proving the request came from your site.

climax.text: SameSite cookies now block most CSRF by default, but legacy applications remain vulnerable.

punchline.text: Your browser's helpfulness is the vulnerability.

quiz.question: What makes CSRF possible?

hook.text: You change the URL from /user/123 to /user/124 and suddenly see someone else's data.

buildup.text: Broken access control means the server doesn't verify if you're allowed to see what you asked for.

discovery.text: OWASP ranked broken access control as the number one web vulnerability in its 2021 list.

twist.text: It's not a coding bug — it's a missing check. The hardest vulnerabilities are the ones you forget.

climax.text: Every endpoint must verify authorization. Assuming the frontend will prevent access is a fatal flaw.

punchline.text: Always check permissions on the server side.

quiz.question: Where should access control be enforced?

hook.text: A developer leaves debug mode on in production. Error pages now show database credentials.

buildup.text: Default passwords, open cloud storage, and verbose error messages are all misconfigurations.

discovery.text: AWS S3 buckets with public read access have leaked millions of records from major companies.

twist.text: The code can be perfectly secure. One wrong setting in the server config undoes everything.

climax.text: Security checklists and automated config scanning prevent the most common deployment mistakes.

punchline.text: One wrong setting can undo perfect code.

quiz.question: What is a common security misconfiguration?
options: Leaving debug mode on in production

hook.text: The most common password in the world is still '123456.' It has been for over a decade.

buildup.text: Users reuse passwords across sites. One breach exposes credentials for dozens of accounts.

discovery.text: Credential stuffing attacks try leaked passwords on other sites — and succeed alarmingly often.

twist.text: Complex password rules don't help. Users just add '!' at the end and capitalize the first letter.

climax.text: Passwords are the weakest link in web security, yet we still rely on them for almost everything.

punchline.text: Humans are terrible at making passwords.

quiz.question: What is the most common password?

hook.text: If a database is stolen, are passwords exposed? Only if they were stored wrong.

buildup.text: Hashing converts a password into a fixed-length string that can't be reversed.

discovery.text: bcrypt and Argon2 add salt — random data — making identical passwords hash differently.

twist.text: MD5 and SHA-1 are too fast for passwords. Attackers can try billions of guesses per second.

climax.text: Slow hashing algorithms like bcrypt make brute-force attacks impractically expensive.

punchline.text: A slow hash is a safe hash.

quiz.question: Why is bcrypt better than MD5 for passwords?
options: It's intentionally slow to resist brute force

hook.text: A password proves you know something. But what if someone else knows it too?

buildup.text: Two-factor authentication adds a second proof — something you have, like a phone.

discovery.text: Time-based codes, push notifications, and hardware keys all serve as second factors.

twist.text: SMS-based 2FA is better than nothing but vulnerable to SIM-swapping attacks.

climax.text: Hardware security keys like YubiKey are nearly impossible to phish — the gold standard.

punchline.text: Two proofs are exponentially harder to steal.

quiz.question: What is the strongest second factor?

hook.text: 'Sign in with Google' is everywhere. But how does a third party verify your identity safely?

buildup.text: OAuth lets users grant limited access to their data without sharing their password.

discovery.text: You authenticate with Google. Google gives the app a token — not your password.

twist.text: OAuth was designed for authorization, not authentication. OpenID Connect fills that gap.

climax.text: Single sign-on reduces password fatigue and centralizes security in trusted providers.

punchline.text: Let the experts handle the login.

quiz.question: What does OAuth share instead of passwords?

hook.text: Apple, Google, and Microsoft agreed on something rare: passwords should die.

buildup.text: Passkeys use public-key cryptography tied to your device — no shared secret to steal.

discovery.text: You authenticate with a fingerprint or face scan. The private key never leaves your device.

twist.text: Passkeys are phishing-resistant by design. The key only works on the real domain.

climax.text: Passkeys may finally end the era of passwords — if adoption reaches critical mass.

punchline.text: Your fingerprint replaces your password.

quiz.question: Where does a passkey's private key live?

hook.text: On HTTP, every message between browser and server travels in plain text anyone can read.

buildup.text: TLS encrypts the connection. HTTPS means your data is scrambled in transit.

discovery.text: Let's Encrypt made TLS certificates free in 2015, removing the biggest barrier to HTTPS.

twist.text: Before Let's Encrypt, certificates cost hundreds of dollars per year. Many sites skipped security.

climax.text: Today browsers mark HTTP sites as 'Not Secure.' HTTPS is the baseline, not a bonus.

punchline.text: Encryption went from luxury to minimum standard.

quiz.question: What did Let's Encrypt change about TLS?

hook.text: What if you could tell the browser exactly which scripts are allowed to run on your page?

buildup.text: Content Security Policy (CSP) is an HTTP header that whitelists trusted content sources.

discovery.text: CSP blocks inline scripts, unauthorized domains, and eval — killing most XSS attacks.

twist.text: Strict CSP breaks many sites at first. Third-party widgets and analytics often violate the policy.

climax.text: CSP is one of the strongest defenses against XSS, but requires careful ongoing maintenance.

punchline.text: A whitelist stops scripts before they run.

quiz.question: What does CSP prevent?

topics.title: CORS: Who Can Talk to Your API

hook.text: Your API has sensitive data. Should any website in the world be able to request it?

buildup.text: The same-origin policy blocks cross-origin requests by default. CORS selectively opens them.

discovery.text: CORS headers tell the browser which domains are allowed to make requests to your server.

twist.text: Setting Access-Control-Allow-Origin to '*' disables the protection entirely — a common mistake.

climax.text: CORS is the web's bouncer. Configure it wrong and everyone gets in.

punchline.text: Wildcard CORS is no CORS at all.

quiz.question: What does CORS control?
options: Which domains can access your API

hook.text: Cookies store session tokens that prove you're logged in. Steal one and you're that user.

buildup.text: The HttpOnly flag prevents JavaScript from reading cookies, blocking XSS-based theft.

discovery.text: Secure flag ensures cookies only travel over HTTPS. SameSite prevents CSRF attacks.

twist.text: Many sites still use cookies without these flags set, leaving sessions exposed to attack.

climax.text: Three simple flags — HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite — prevent the majority of cookie attacks.

punchline.text: Three flags protect your sessions from most attacks.

quiz.question: What does the HttpOnly flag do?

hook.text: The EU's GDPR fined companies billions for mishandling personal data since 2018.

buildup.text: GDPR requires explicit consent, data minimization, and the right to be forgotten.

discovery.text: Users can request all data a company holds on them — and demand its complete deletion.

twist.text: GDPR applies to any site with EU visitors, regardless of where the company is based.

climax.text: Privacy regulation turned data protection from a best practice into a legal obligation worldwide.

punchline.text: Collect less data and sleep better at night.

quiz.question: What does GDPR give users the right to?

topics.title: The Yahoo Breach: Three Billion Accounts

hook.text: In 2013, every single Yahoo account was compromised. All three billion of them.

buildup.text: Attackers accessed names, emails, phone numbers, and hashed passwords for every user.

discovery.text: Yahoo didn't disclose the breach until 2016 — three years after it happened.

twist.text: The breach was revealed during Verizon's acquisition. Yahoo's price dropped $350 million.

climax.text: The Yahoo breach remains the largest data breach in history by number of affected accounts.

punchline.text: Three billion accounts, three years of silence.

quiz.question: How many Yahoo accounts were breached?

hook.text: In 2017, hackers stole Social Security numbers for 147 million Americans from Equifax.

buildup.text: The attackers exploited a known vulnerability in Apache Struts that had a patch available.

discovery.text: Equifax knew about the vulnerability but failed to apply the patch for over two months.

twist.text: The breach check website Equifax created had its own security flaws and served wrong information.

climax.text: Equifax paid over $700 million in settlements. The CEO resigned. Patching would have cost nothing.

punchline.text: A free patch would have prevented a $700M fine.

quiz.question: What caused the Equifax breach?

hook.text: In 2013, hackers stole 40 million credit card numbers from Target during the holiday season.

buildup.text: The attackers entered through a third-party HVAC contractor with network access.

discovery.text: Malware on point-of-sale systems captured card data as customers swiped at checkout.

twist.text: Target's security system flagged the intrusion. The alerts were ignored by the team.

climax.text: Target spent over $200 million on the breach. The CIO and CEO both resigned.

punchline.text: The alarm went off; nobody listened.

quiz.question: How did attackers enter Target's network?

hook.text: In 2020, hackers compromised SolarWinds' software update system used by 18,000 organizations.

buildup.text: Malicious code was inserted into a legitimate software update that customers installed trustingly.

discovery.text: US government agencies, Fortune 500 companies, and security firms were all compromised.

twist.text: The attack went undetected for nine months. The attackers had access the entire time.

climax.text: SolarWinds showed that supply chain trust is one of cybersecurity's hardest unsolved problems.

punchline.text: Trusted updates delivered the attack itself.

quiz.question: How was the SolarWinds attack delivered?

hook.text: In December 2021, a flaw in a Java logging library put half the internet at risk overnight.

buildup.text: Log4j was used by millions of servers. A simple text string could trigger remote code execution.

discovery.text: Attackers could take complete control of a server by typing a crafted string into a search box.

twist.text: Log4j was maintained by a handful of unpaid volunteers. Critical infrastructure ran on free labor.

climax.text: Log4Shell exposed how fragile the web's foundations are when key libraries are under-resourced.

punchline.text: Free software supported the world but not itself.

quiz.question: What was Log4Shell?
options: A vulnerability in a widely used Java logging library

hook.text: A castle has walls, a moat, guards, and a locked treasury. Web security works the same way.

buildup.text: Defense in depth layers multiple security controls so no single failure is catastrophic.

discovery.text: Firewalls, input validation, authentication, and encryption each stop different attacks.

twist.text: If your only defense is a strong password, one phishing email takes down everything.

climax.text: Layered security means an attacker must beat every defense, not just the weakest one.

punchline.text: One wall isn't enough; layer your defenses.

quiz.question: What is defense in depth?

hook.text: Every piece of data from a user is potentially hostile. Treat it that way.

buildup.text: Validation checks that input matches expected formats — numbers, emails, dates.

discovery.text: Sanitization strips dangerous characters before data reaches the database or the page.

twist.text: Client-side validation improves UX but provides zero security. Attackers bypass it trivially.

climax.text: Server-side validation is the only real barrier. Never trust what arrives from the browser.

punchline.text: Validate on the server; everything else is cosmetic.

quiz.question: Why is client-side validation insufficient for security?

hook.text: An attacker tries 10,000 password combinations per second against your login form.

buildup.text: Rate limiting caps the number of requests from a single source in a given time window.

discovery.text: After five failed logins, lock the account temporarily. Simple but devastatingly effective.

twist.text: Sophisticated attackers rotate IP addresses. CAPTCHAs and device fingerprinting counter this.

climax.text: Rate limiting is the simplest defense against brute force and one of the most neglected.

punchline.text: Slow down attackers and they'll move on.

quiz.question: What does rate limiting prevent?

hook.text: HTTP response headers can activate powerful browser security features at zero cost.

buildup.text: Strict-Transport-Security forces HTTPS. X-Frame-Options blocks clickjacking attacks.

discovery.text: X-Content-Type-Options stops browsers from guessing file types — a common attack vector.

twist.text: Most sites are missing at least three critical security headers. The defaults are insecure.

climax.text: Adding security headers takes minutes and blocks entire categories of attacks automatically.

punchline.text: A few headers block entire attack categories.

quiz.question: What does Strict-Transport-Security do?
options: Forces the browser to use HTTPS

topics.title: Security Is a Process Not a Product

hook.text: You can't buy a product and declare your website secure. Security is ongoing work.

buildup.text: New vulnerabilities are discovered daily. Dependencies need updating. Threats evolve.

discovery.text: Penetration testing, dependency audits, and security training must happen continuously.

twist.text: The most secure organizations assume they will be breached and plan for containment.

climax.text: Security culture — where every developer thinks about threats — is the strongest defense of all.

punchline.text: Security is a habit, not a checkbox.

quiz.question: What is the strongest security defense?
